newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE - Film "Crash" runs into moral barrier in Britain.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Film "Crash" runs into moral barrier in Britain.

text.p: "Crash", a film about car accidents and sexual desire, has hit the barriers of British censorship and become the latest focus of a political battle over morality.
Awarded the Jury Prize at this year's Cannes film festival for its "audacity, daring and originality", "Crash" had a mixed response at its London Film Festival screening.
"Crash" hinges on a couple who survive a car accident, find it erotic and indulge in roadside sex. Since its festival showing, the film has been seized on by the right-wing press.

One critic said it was "beyond the depths of depravity" and it has already been banned from central London's cinemas. Film censors are discussing over whether to grant "Crash" a viewing certificate at all.

The British are markedly different in their approach to sex and art from their continental European neighbours who have a more relaxed attitude. "Crash" is the latest example of soul-searching which dates back to the debate over the morality of publishing D.H. Lawrence's "Lady Chatterley's Lover".

"The film is sexual but not violent," said its Canadian director David Cronenberg, renowned for turning horror into high art. "I don't think somebody is going to see this film, copy it and go and look for car crashes to get off on."
Starring James Spader, of "sex, lies and videotape", and Holly Hunter of "The Piano", "Crash" has been well received in France and Canada.
Cronenberg, best known for the science fiction film "The Fly", said "Crash" was a "strange existentialist romance" and "experimental and complex but not a social danger".

Britain's Heritage Secretary Virginia Bottomley disagrees -- strongly. She has urged local authorities to ban the film even if the British Board of Film Classification (BBFC) gives it a certificate allowing only those over 18 to watch it.
The unpopular Conservative government, in power since 1979 and facing an election by May, recently launched an initiative to curb sex and violence in videos and on the "silver screen".
Mary Whitehouse, influential former president of the watchdog National Viewers' and Listeners' Association, echoed Bottomley's call, labelling the film "crazy, sick and wicked".

Both the Conservatives and opposition Labour Party are tussling over morality -- be it restoring discipline in schools, tightening gun laws, removing sleaze from parliament -- and "Crash" has become part of the political discussion.
"There is a sort of phantom invented version of this movie that exists only to be a political pawn. My movie has somehow become a pawn in the politics of the United Kingdom," Cronenberg said.
"We have been caught up in the electioneering between the political parties." said J.G Ballard, British author of the 1973 novel that inspired the film.

Westminster Council ruled the film could not be seen in London's entertainment district. The council will review the ban once the 22 BBFC board members have decided whether or not to release the film, said council chairman John Bull.
"It's a good film. It's exceedingly well made (but) I could live without it," Bull said. Other councillors expressed concern that films like "Crash" could spur copycat crimes.

The BBFC is busy compiling a report, requested by Home Secretary (interior minister) Michael Howard, on measures it is taking to reduce the level of violence in videos. The report is due on December 6, one BBFC official said.
More than 50 leading film makers have spoken out against the council's call for three scenes to be cut.
One shows a man making love to a woman wearing callipers. Another shows a sex act involving a bruised, bleeding woman.
"I would not want the film shown in Britain if it has to be cut, but whether I have the power to do that is another matter," said Cronenberg.

Ballard defended scenes in both the book and the film re-enacting crashes in which famous people were killed. The deaths of people like James Dean and Jayne Mansfield "have a certain resonance", he said.

Sony subsidiary Columbia Tristar, the film's British distributor, had hoped to release the film at 100 British cinemas in January. Local authorities have the power to overrule any decision made by the BBFC, as some did with U.S. director Martin Scorcese's controversial "Last Temptation of Christ".
Britain's Daily Mail, a right-wing tabloid that sees itself as the voice of the silent, moral majority, called for a ban of "Crash", and urged directors to exercise self-restraint.
It cited Stanley Kubrick's self-imposed ban on showing "Clockwork Orange" in Britain after youths copied a scene from his film, raping a woman while singing "Singing in the Rain".
"Natural Born Killers", which director Oliver Stone defended as a satire on what he called "modern society's obsession with serial murder", was granted an 18 certificate by the board.
Warner Home Videos withdrew the film the day after a massacre at Dublane in Scotland, in which 16 children and their teacher were killed in a school.
